draft.title: Models and meters
card: The water-in-pipes model helps explain circuits. Wires are pipes, charge is the water, and a battery is a pump that pushes it round. Current is like the flow rate, and voltage is like the pressure that drives the flow.
Every model has limits. Water can leak out of a pipe, but charge does not leak out of a wire in a complete circuit. The model also does not show why a lamp glows.
measures current. It is placed in series, so the current passes through it. A good ammeter has very low resistance so it barely changes the current.
measures potential difference. It is placed in parallel across the part being tested, so it compares the two ends. A good voltmeter has very high resistance so it draws almost no current.
draft.remember: Ammeter in series to measure current. Voltmeter in parallel to measure voltage.

a.q: In the water-in-pipes model of a simple circuit, what does the battery correspond to?
opts: A pump that pushes the water round
A narrow section that slows the flow
A tap that controls how much flows
A tank that stores water for later use
a.why: The battery gives charge the energy to move round the circuit, as a pump does for water. A tap or narrow pipe would act more like something that restricts flow, not something that drives it.
a.clue: Which part of a water system pushes the water along?

b.q: Priya wants to measure the current through a lamp and the voltage across it. How should she connect the meters?
opts: Ammeter in series, voltmeter across the lamp
Ammeter across the lamp, voltmeter in series
Both meters in series with the lamp
Both meters in parallel across the lamp
b.why: Current must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series. A voltmeter compares the two ends of the lamp, so it goes in parallel. Putting the ammeter across the lamp is tempting because both meters touch the lamp, but it would not measure the current through the lamp.
b.clue: One meter must let the current pass through it. The other compares two points.

a.best: A pump that pushes the water round

b.best: Ammeter in series, voltmeter across the lamp

problems.detail: The clue 'Which part of a water system pushes the water along?' uses the same verb as the right option ('pushes the water round'), so a student can match the words without knowing the model.

check.summary: The physics is correct and both questions have one clear answer. The only problem is that question a's clue repeats the word 'pushes' from the right option, which gives the answer away.
